sent: This work investigates how an object detector small enough for embedded hardware can be trained when real training images are scarce, using wildlife species recognition as the test case. The deployment context is a consumer binocular that classifies the mammal a user is looking at, on the device itself, and without a network connection. That fixes two hard constraints: a per-frame latency budget on a mobile system-on-chip, and a class universe of 225 mammal species rather than the few dozen coarse classes of a general detection benchmark. The detector has to locate the animal and classify its species, and classification carries the difficulty, since many of these species differ only in fine markings (ZQX0ZQX). Two training strategies are compared: distilling a much larger fine-tuned teacher model into a small student model and fine-tuning that same student directly on the wildlife dataset. Of the 225 classes, 50 retain fewer than 150 usable real photographs each, so this work also asks whether diffusion-generated imagery can provide the missing real data, and how far a detector trained on it still transfers to real photographs.

sent: Species identification in the field has begun to move from printed field guides into the optics themselves. The AX Visio binocular runs a species-recognition model on board and classifies the animal the user is already looking at. The classification must happen while the animal is still within the field of view. This rules out sending the frame to a remote service. The habitats in which the device is used also rule this out, since network coverage cannot be assumed there. The recognition model therefore has to fit a mobile system-on-chip and meet a per-frame latency budget on it. The deployment target is the Qualcomm QCS605, a mobile platform combining a Hexagon 685 digital signal processor with an Adreno 615 graphics processor, whose compute budget excludes the model scales at which detection accuracy is normally reported. Development and benchmarking in this work targeted a Raspberry Pi 400 instead, for the software-maturity reasons set out in ZQX0ZQX.

sent: Accurate detection comes at the cost of model size and inference speed. The most accurate models are large, which makes an embedded target difficult to achieve. The teacher model used in this study has approximately 193 M parameters, compared to 2.71 M for the student model that was actually exported to the device. Knowledge distillation is the established solution to such a discrepancy. Early work on model compression trained a small, fast model to reproduce the outputs of a large ensemble. Later work generalized the idea by having the student match the teacher's softened output distribution rather than its hard predictions. Whether that mechanism survives a move from general object classes to fine-grained species is the question this work was built around.

sent: In wildlife monitoring, recognizing an animal's species automatically is difficult when the recognition must run on a battery-powered device carried into the field. Such a device cannot host the large models that perform best on this task, and photographs are plentiful for a few familiar animals and scarce for most others. The model in use is an object detector, which locates the animal in the frame and assigns it a species. The difficulty lies in that classification rather than in the localization, because many species differ only in fine markings. This thesis examines how a compact detector should be trained under those two constraints, and what the available data allows.

sent: A training dataset is assembled from openly licensed photographs and curated automatically. Species that remain poorly represented are supplemented with generated images, and several image generators are compared beforehand to find which produces the most useful training material. The compact detector is then trained twice, once by distilling a much larger fine-tuned model into it and once directly on the same data, and the speed of both is measured on hardware comparable to the intended device.

sent: The comparison finds no advantage for distillation over direct training, least of all for the species whose training data is thinnest. Neither the apparent realism of the generated images nor their price predicts how useful they prove. How much descriptive detail the generator is given matters more than which generator is chosen. Replacing part of a small set of real photographs with generated images proves harmless, while replacing all of them does not. Accuracy measured on generated test images overstates accuracy on real ones, a discrepancy this work reports rather than corrects. The resulting detector misses the intended device's speed budget by an order of magnitude, since no compression step was applied yet, and closing that gap is left to future work.

sent: Two properties of the wildlife domain make that question non-trivial. The class universe is fine-grained: many of the 225 classes differ only in fine markings, and a detector has to learn exactly those markings. The available imagery is long-tailed, with a few well-photographed species dominating the corpus while most are supported by comparatively few usable photographs. Machine-learning work on wildlife imagery treats both properties as recurring obstacles rather than as edge cases. Camera-trap detection is also known to degrade sharply once a model is evaluated at locations it was not trained on, so a thin per-class image pool is a generalization problem and not only a sample-count problem.

sent: Text-to-image diffusion models offer the one intervention that can add appearance content a data-poor class's own photographs do not contain, such as an unrecorded pose, habitat or lighting condition. Training a classifier from scratch on generated images, however, required roughly five times as many of them to match real images of the same classes, and prompting an off-the-shelf generator with bare class names produced a very poor classifier. Earlier work by the present author found that generated image context conferred no downstream detection advantage over per-pixel random noise on a small-object car-detection task, which is what leaves the choice of generator an open question here (ZQX0ZQX). Synthetic imagery is therefore treated in this work as a supplement whose usefulness is measured rather than assumed.

sent: Ein Fernglas, das die Tierart benennt, die der Nutzer gerade betrachtet, muss diese Aufgabe auf dem Gerät selbst lösen, denn im Gelände ist eine Netzverbindung nicht gegeben. Daraus ergeben sich zwei Einschränkungen. Der batteriebetriebene Prozessor kann die großen Modelle nicht ausführen, die bei der Detektion und Klassifikation von Wildtieren die besten Ergebnisse erzielen. Zugleich sind Fotografien von wenigen bekannten Tieren im Überfluss vorhanden, von den meisten übrigen Arten dagegen nur in geringer Zahl. Das eingesetzte Modell ist ein Objektdetektor, der das Tier im Bild findet und ihm eine Art zuordnet. Die eigentliche Schwierigkeit liegt dabei nicht in der Detektion des Tieres, sondern in der Klassifikation der Tierart, da sich viele Arten nur in feinen Merkmalen unterscheiden. Diese Arbeit untersucht, wie ein kompakter Detektor unter diesen Bedingungen trainiert werden sollte und was die verfügbaren Daten zulassen.

sent: Der Vergleich zeigt keinen Vorteil der Knowledge Distillation gegenüber dem direkten Fine-Tuning, am wenigsten bei den Arten mit den knappsten Trainingsdaten. Wie nützlich die generierten Bilder für das Training sind, lässt sich weder an ihrem augenscheinlichen Realismus noch an ihrem Preis ablesen. Größeren Einfluss als die Wahl des Generators hat, wie ausführlich die Bildbeschreibung ist, die ihm vorgegeben wird. Wird ein Teil eines kleinen Bestands realer Fotografien durch generierte Bilder ersetzt, bleibt die Genauigkeit unverändert. Wird der gesamte Bestand ersetzt, sinkt sie. Auf generierten Testbildern fällt die gemessene Genauigkeit höher aus als auf realen Fotografien. Diese Abweichung legt die Arbeit offen, behebt sie aber nicht. Der entstandene Detektor ist für das Zeitbudget des vorgesehenen Geräts noch um eine Größenordnung zu langsam, da bislang kein Kompressionsschritt angewandt wurde. Das Schließen dieser Lücke bleibt künftiger Arbeit überlassen.
